situation.text: Hoje você conhece Cole, de Miami. Senha, sinal e problemas simples.

pages.goal: Hoje você aprende a avisar de defeitos: Penny, the oven is not working. Oh no! The bulb is broken too, Uncle. The faucet is not working. No water!

pages.hook: In many American homes, cafés and hotels, guests ask for the Wi-Fi name and password in the first minutes. Learn the words and the small talk that go with it.
pages.polite: Ask first: **“Could I get the Wi-Fi password, please?”** Then say **thanks**. A short **“Sorry to bother you”** is also nice.

mythfact.s: Many cafés in the USA have a Wi-Fi name and a password on a sign or on the receipt.
mythfact.why: Often the password is on the wall, on the menu or on your receipt, or you can ask the staff.

mythfact.s: A router is the box that sends the Wi-Fi signal around the house.
mythfact.why: The router connects your devices to the internet.

mythfact.s: Wi-Fi and the internet are exactly the same thing.
mythfact.why: Wi-Fi is a wireless way to connect to the network. The internet is the big network itself.

mythfact.s: “Turn it off and on again” is a very common first tip for tech problems.
mythfact.why: Restarting a router or phone often fixes small problems, so people say it a lot.

mythfact.s: You must always pay to use Wi-Fi in a hotel.
mythfact.why: Many hotels offer free Wi-Fi, but some charge extra. You can check at the front desk.

compare.br: In Brazil many people ask “Qual é a senha do Wi-Fi?” in a café or at a friend’s home, and the staff often just tell you the password.
compare.us: In the USA it is the same, but people often start with “Do you have Wi-Fi?” and then ask for the password. Some places print it on the receipt.
compare.tip: Say the password slowly, letter by letter. In English, “capital A” means a big letter.
compare.ask: How do you ask for the Wi-Fi password where you live? Say it in English.

pages.title: Reading quest — The Wi-Fi is down!
text: Sam works from home in Miami. One morning he opens his laptop and sees a message: “No internet.” He says, “**The Wi-Fi is down!** Ugh, the worst.”
His sister Lia comes in. “What happened?” she asks. “**It’s not working**,” says Sam. “Look at the router! The light is red.” Lia **looks at** the small box and smiles.

She remembers a funny old cartoon, **Inspector Gadget**. It is an animated series from 1983. The detective has many gadgets, but they often do not work, and his clever niece Penny fixes the problem. “Sam,” says Lia, “you are like the inspector today.”
Then she says, “**Turn it off and on again.**” Sam pulls out the plug. They wait ten seconds. Then he plugs it in again. The light is yellow, then green.
Sam opens the laptop. “**Great!** It works!” he shouts. “You’re a genius.” Lia laughs. “No, I just know the first trick.”
Now Sam writes the password on a small card and puts it next to the router. “Next time,” he says, “I can try resetting it by myself.”
